Name: analogical_transfer_gate
Title: Solved It Once, Solving It Again: An Internal Analogy Gate Governing Whether Reasoning Models Reuse a Worked Example or Re-Derive From Scratch
Short Hypothesis: When shown a fully-worked solution to a structurally-identical problem immediately before the target, reasoning models frequently FAIL to transfer the method—re-deriving from scratch and wasting large numbers of tokens—and, mirroring human analogical transfer, this failure is modulated by surface vs. structural similarity. The transfer-vs-re-derivation decision is governed by an internal, linearly-decodable analogy-gate signal that fires (or fails to fire) at the moment the target problem begins; steering it causally flips the model between reuse and re-derivation.
Related Work: Two previously-disconnected literatures. (1) Interpretability of in-context task reuse: Circuit Component Reuse Across Tasks (2023) and Function Induction (2025) show internal components/circuits are shared across tasks; Just-in-time and Distributed Task Representations (2025) shows transferrable task vectors form sporadically at specific tokens; task-vector work extracts task identity from activations. (2) Cognitive science on analogical transfer (Structure-Mapping Theory) documents that humans reuse solutions to structurally-similar problems, with success gated by surface vs. structural similarity and by retrieval failure. Crucially, NO prior work asks the *behavioral* question we pose: does a reasoning model reuse its OWN just-seen worked solution on a new instance of the same problem, or wastefully re-derive—and how much compute does this cost? Circuit-reuse work studies static shared components, not the dynamic in-context decision to transfer; systems-level activation/KV caching reuses computation externally without asking whether the model itself recognizes the analogy. Our contribution is (a) quantifying in-context analogical-transfer failure in reasoning LLMs as wasted reasoning tokens, (b) showing it is modulated by surface vs. structural similarity as in human analogy, and (c) locating and causally steering an internal analogy gate—plausibly a just-in-time signal at target onset—that switches between reuse and re-derivation. This differs from all my prior proposals, which concern within-single-problem overthinking.
Abstract: Humans who have just solved a problem reuse the method when they meet a structurally identical one, thinking far less the second time. We ask whether reasoning language models do the same. We present a reasoning model with a fully-worked solution to a problem, then a target that is structurally identical but differs in surface details (numbers, cover story, variable names), and measure whether the model transfers the method (short, reuse-style reasoning) or re-derives from scratch (long, redundant reasoning). We hypothesize that models frequently fail to transfer, wasting tokens, and—mirroring human analogy—that transfer succeeds more with high surface similarity and fails when only deep structure is shared, while a surface-similar-but-structurally-different distractor induces harmful reuse. Across GSM8K, MATH500, and templated algorithmic word problems on open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 distills 1.5B-14B, Qwen3), we quantify a transfer-failure rate and its dependence on surface vs. structural similarity. We then test a mechanistic account: at the token boundary where the target begins, the residual stream linearly encodes an analogy-gate signal predicting reuse vs. re-derivation. We train probes for this signal, test its separability from raw target difficulty, localize the carrying components via activation patching (patching the analogy-recognition state from a transfer-inducing context into a re-derivation context), and causally steer the gate to flip behavior with specificity controls. Finally we turn the gate into a training-free intervention that induces reuse when a valid analog is present, cutting tokens at equal accuracy. Our work reframes a slice of overthinking as analogical-transfer failure with an identifiable, steerable internal cause.
Experiments: 1) Construct analog sets: For each seed problem generate (a) a surface-similar structural analog (same solution method and cover story, different numbers), (b) a structure-only analog (same method, different domain/cover story), and (c) a surface-similar structurally-different distractor (similar wording, different method). Seeds from GSM8K, MATH500, and templated algorithmic word problems where the method is well-defined. Verify structural equivalence by matching solution-step templates plus human/LLM-judge checks; verify difficulty parity via pass-rate matching. 2) Quantify transfer behavior: Present [worked solution to analog] + [target] and measure target reasoning-token count and accuracy, vs. baselines [target alone] and [irrelevant worked solution + target]. Define transfer-success = substantial token reduction with retained accuracy vs. no-analog baseline; transfer-failure = re-derivation (token count comparable to no-analog). Metrics: transfer-failure rate, mean token reduction, accuracy per condition. Hypotheses: high overall failure rate; lower failure for surface-similar than structure-only analogs; distractor induces harmful reuse (accuracy drop)—mirroring human surface-vs-structure effects. 3) Analogy-gate probing (Location): At the token boundary where the target begins (after the worked example, before any target reasoning token), extract residual-stream activations; train per-layer linear probes to predict transfer vs. re-derivation. Metrics: AUROC/accuracy, layer sweep. Baselines to establish separability from confounds: (i) a difficulty probe trained on target pass-rate, (ii) a surface-overlap feature baseline, (iii) prior-text bag-of-words. Key claim: gate predicts transfer above and beyond difficulty and surface overlap; test via principal angles between gate and difficulty directions and partial correlation. Also test the just-in-time hypothesis: whether the gate is decodable only near target onset (temporal locality) vs. throughout. 4) Causal patching (Causal Intervention): For a fixed target/method, patch the prompt-boundary activation from a surface-similar (transfer-inducing) context into a structure-only (re-derivation) context and measure whether the model switches to reuse (token drop, method-matched solution). Report sign, dose (layer subset/strength), specificity (matched-random-direction control; off-target accuracy preserved). 5) Gate steering (Causal Intervention): Derive an analogy-gate steering direction (difference-of-means between transfer and re-derivation boundary states). Steer up to induce reuse when a valid analog is present; steer down as control. Measure token reduction and accuracy; verify steering does NOT induce harmful reuse of the distractor (specificity). 6) Training-free efficiency application: When a valid worked analog is in context, apply gate steering to induce reuse; evaluate tokens-at-equal-accuracy vs. no intervention and vs. prompting ('reuse the method above'). 7) Generalization: transfer probe and steering across datasets and model scales without retraining; test cross-domain analogs (a math method reused in a physics word problem).
Risk Factors and Limitations: The analogy gate may be inseparable from raw difficulty or surface-overlap features, weakening the mechanistic claim; the separability analysis, patching, and distractor-specificity tests directly address this, and a null would still yield a novel behavioral characterization of transfer failure. Constructing clean structural analogs that hold difficulty constant while varying surface similarity is nontrivial; we mitigate with template-based generation and human/LLM verification plus pass-rate matching. Transfer-success detection relies on token-count and method-match, which are noisy; we use both token-reduction and step-template matching and validate with human spot-checks. Inducing reuse could cause harmful transfer to structurally-different distractors (accuracy loss); the distractor condition and steering-specificity metric quantify this trade-off. Reasoning-length measurement requires clear think/answer delimiters. Effects and the strength of surface-vs-structure modulation may be model-family and scale specific, and cross-domain transfer may be rare in smaller models (itself an informative result).
